homePage.heroSubtitle: Your everyday calculator for social media, video, photography and screens
homePage.whatIsAspectRatioText: An aspect ratio describes the proportional relationship between width and height. Written as W:H (e.g., 16:9), it tells you the shape of a screen, image, or video frame. A 16:9 ratio means for every 16 units of width, the height is 9 units — the standard for HD and 4K video. A 1:1 ratio is a perfect square, used for Instagram feed posts.
homePage.howToUseStep1Text: Enter your original dimensions (the ratio locks automatically), then type a new width or height — the other dimension calculates instantly. Pick a platform preset to auto-fill recommended dimensions.
homePage.howToUseStep2Text: Enter any width and height to discover the simplified ratio, decimal value, closest standard match, and CSS padding-bottom value. Upload an image to instantly detect its dimensions.
homePage.howToUseStep3Text: Upload any image and choose where you want to use it — social media, websites, print, or personal use. Get instant recommendations with crop analysis and one-click dimension copying.

aboutPage.title: About
aboutPage.heading: About the Aspect Ratio Calculator
aboutPage.lead: A free tool for working out aspect ratios and resizing to them without guesswork. No account, no upload, no cost.
aboutPage.purpose: Aspect ratio sits underneath a lot of work that is not about aspect ratio. A photograph that needs cropping. A slide that has to fill a projector. A television bought for the kind of films you actually watch. A container that needs an exact height in code. In every one of those the decision is the same small piece of arithmetic, and getting it wrong shows immediately: something is too big, too small, soft, or surrounded by space that should not be there. Some of that you can fix by eye. Code you cannot — it wants a number. This site exists to make that decision quickly and then get out of the way.
aboutPage.whatItDoes: Three things. The calculator resizes a width or a height while holding a ratio fixed. Find-ratio takes any two dimensions and tells you the ratio they make, reduced to its simplest form. The Image Wizard takes an image, reads its dimensions automatically, and shows how it will crop on each major social platform.
aboutPage.privacy: Every calculation runs in your browser. Images opened in the Image Wizard are read locally and are never uploaded, stored or transmitted — there is no server to send them to. The site also installs as an app and keeps working with no connection at all.
aboutPage.languages: The calculator, the guides and the platform reference pages are published in English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, Japanese, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Arabic, Ukrainian, Polish, Romanian and Vietnamese.
aboutPage.maintenance: Social platform dimensions change, so the platform pages are reviewed against each platform's own published specification rather than copied from other guides. Every article carries the date it was published, and that date is only moved when the words actually change.
aboutPage.contactCta: Found something wrong, or something missing?

contactPage.heading: Contact

contactPage.feedback: The feedback form is the fastest route. It takes a message and, optionally, what you use the calculator for — which is what decides what gets built next.
contactPage.security: Security reports follow RFC 9116. The machine-readable contact details are published at /.well-known/security.txt, and reports sent through the feedback form reach the same place.
contactPage.data: Nothing you calculate is transmitted, so there is nothing to request or delete. What the site does collect, and how to turn it off, is set out in the privacy policy.

developersPage.title: API
developersPage.heading: Developer API
developersPage.lead: The calculator is callable. No key, no account, no rate limit beyond ordinary fair use — and every response says where it came from.
developersPage.ratio: Give it a width and a height and it returns the simplified ratio. Give it a ratio and one dimension and it returns the other. Give it nothing and it lists every named ratio on the site.
developersPage.content: Every content page has a JSON representation of the same resource. You can request it directly, or ask for it on the page's own URL by sending an Accept header of application/json — the HTML and the JSON are the same thing in two forms.
developersPage.spec: The full OpenAPI 3.1 description of both endpoints, so a client can be generated rather than written.
developersPage.cors: Cross-origin requests are allowed from anywhere. The responses are public arithmetic over public data — there is no session and nothing here that is not already on the page.
developersPage.terms: Free to use, including commercially, with attribution to aspect-ratio-calculator.com. If the API saves you building your own, a link back is the whole price.

safeZoneTool.title: Instagram Reels Safe Zone Checker — Free
safeZoneTool.description: Check what Instagram Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts cover on your 1080 × 1920 frame — and how much width the phone screen itself cuts off.
safeZoneTool.h1: Safe zone checker for Reels, TikTok and Shorts
safeZoneTool.answer: A safe zone is the part of a 1080 × 1920 frame that nothing covers. Instagram Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts each reserve different margins for captions, buttons and the profile bar. There is a second loss almost nobody accounts for: modern phone screens are taller than 9:16, so a correctly sized Reel is scaled up to fill the screen and roughly 18% of its width is pushed off the edges — about 97 pixels per side on an iPhone 15. No export setting changes that; you frame for it.
safeZoneTool.fact1: The canvas is the same 1080 × 1920 on all three platforms. What differs is how much of it the app paints over.
safeZoneTool.fact2: The screen crop is arithmetic, not opinion: a 9:16 video is 1.78 times taller than wide, an iPhone 15 screen is 2.17, and filling the screen top to bottom pushes the difference off the sides.
safeZoneTool.fact3: On a genuine 9:16 screen the crop is exactly zero, which is the check that the formula is right.
safeZoneTool.showCrop: Show the screen crop on the frame
safeZoneTool.frameAlt: Safe area on a {w} by {h} frame
safeZoneTool.screenDominates: On this phone the screen takes more width than the interface does. Designing to the published safe zone alone would still lose {px} px a side.
safeZoneTool.provenanceOurs: The screen crop is computed here from each phone's published resolution — you can check it: scale 1080 × 1920 until its height matches the screen, and whatever the width exceeds the screen by is what you lose. A true 9:16 screen returns zero, which is the test that the formula is right.
safeZoneTool.provenanceNotOurs: The interface margins are not ours.
safeZoneTool.provenanceUnverified: , and not yet verified against a current build by us
safeZoneTool.provenanceMoves: Platforms move these without announcing it, so treat them as a guide and the arithmetic as the guarantee.
safeZoneTool.reelsTop: status bar and the Reels/Following switcher
safeZoneTool.reelsBottom: username, caption, audio ticker and the progress bar
safeZoneTool.reelsSides: the like / comment / share / audio rail down the right
safeZoneTool.reelsSource: ARC's own platform copy, which states a 1080×1420 centred safe area with 250px reserved top and bottom. Side figures are the conventional values for the action rail and have not been measured here.
safeZoneTool.tiktokBottom: username, caption, music title — TikTok's caption block is the deepest of the three and it grows with the caption
safeZoneTool.tiktokSides: avatar, like, comment, bookmark, share and the spinning record
safeZoneTool.tiktokSource: Conventional published values; not measured against a build here.
safeZoneTool.shortsBottom: channel name, title, and the Subscribe button
safeZoneTool.shortsSides: like, dislike, comments, share, remix and the sound disc
safeZoneTool.shortsSource: Conventional published values; not measured against a build here.
safeZoneTool.tagline: What Reels, TikTok and Shorts cover, and what the screen cuts.

phoneCropTool.title: Why Is Instagram Cropping My Reel? — Free Checker
phoneCropTool.description: Your export is a correct 9:16 — the crop happens on the phone screen after that. See the exact loss for your phone, in pixels, and what to frame for instead.
phoneCropTool.h1: Why does Instagram crop my Reel even though I exported 9:16?
phoneCropTool.answer: A correctly exported 9:16 Reel still gets cropped because phone screens are taller than 9:16 — an iPhone 15's screen is 2.168:1 — and Instagram scales the video up to fill the screen top to bottom, pushing 18.0% of its width off the edges, 97 pixels a side. No export setting changes it and there is no fix: the only workaround is to frame the shot so nothing that has to be read sits in that outer margin.
phoneCropTool.fact1: The crop is arithmetic, not a bug: a 1080×1920 export is 1.778 wide-to-tall, an iPhone 15's screen is 2.168, and scaling the video to fill the screen's height pushes 18.0% of its width off the edges — 97 pixels a side.
phoneCropTool.fact2: A screen at exactly 9:16 crops nothing: the same formula returns 0.0% loss for that case, which is the check that it is arithmetic and not a guess.
phoneCropTool.fact3: There is no export setting that fixes this, because the loss happens on the phone's glass after the file is already correct — the fix is framing the shot so nothing essential sits in the lost margin.
phoneCropTool.frameAlt: A {w} by {h} export, with the part a phone screen crops shaded
phoneCropTool.noCrop: 0.0% — the control: a true 9:16 screen loses nothing
phoneCropTool.noFixNeeded: This screen is exactly 9:16, so there is nothing to fix here — the crop only exists on screens taller than the video.
phoneCropTool.noFixExists: There is no export setting that fixes this. The loss happens on the phone's screen, after your file is already the correct 1080×1920 — reinstalling the app or changing an export preset changes nothing.
phoneCropTool.whatToDoText: Frame the shot so nothing essential — a face, a caption, on-screen text — sits in the outer {pct} on either side; that's the strip this screen's shape pushes off the glass.
phoneCropTool.whatToDoTextZero: Nothing to frame around here — a true 9:16 screen keeps the whole width, edge to edge.
phoneCropTool.quoteText: Why does Instagram zoom in reels after they're posted? ... parts of the video are cut off. I can't find an answer anywhere. I'm uploading the correct ratio 9:16.
phoneCropTool.quoteSource: — a real, still-unanswered question, posted on Threads
phoneCropTool.tagline: The 18% a phone screen takes off a correct 9:16 upload.

pixelsInchesTool.title: Pixels to Inches Calculator — Print Size at Any DPI
pixelsInchesTool.description: Enter a pixel width and height to get the exact print size in inches and centimeters at 300, 150 and 72 DPI — and see why a screen has no real DPI.
pixelsInchesTool.h1: Pixels to inches: print size at any DPI
pixelsInchesTool.answer: Pixels convert to inches with one division: inches equals pixels divided by DPI, so a 3000-pixel-wide image is exactly 10 inches at 300 DPI, the standard for printing photos and documents up close. The same pixels stretch to 20 inches at 150 DPI, the accepted floor for a poster or banner viewed from further back. A screen has no DPI in this sense at all — pixel density varies by display and has nothing to do with how many pixels a file contains, which is why the '72 DPI' figure people quote for screens is a leftover print convention, not a measurement of anything on your monitor.
pixelsInchesTool.fact1: The arithmetic is one division: inches equals pixels divided by DPI. A 3000-pixel-wide image is exactly 10 inches at 300 DPI — no rounding, because 3000 divided by 300 is a whole number.
pixelsInchesTool.fact2: 300 DPI is the commercial standard for printing photos and documents viewed up close. 150 DPI is the accepted floor for large-format prints — posters and banners — because they're viewed from further away, so the eye can't resolve as many dots per inch.
pixelsInchesTool.fact3: 72 DPI is a legacy screen figure from the original 1984 Macintosh, whose screen was built to match 72 points per inch. No screen sold today has that pixel density, and the number says nothing about how sharp an image looks on any real display.
pixelsInchesTool.fact4: The same pixel count prints at different sizes depending only on the DPI you choose: a 3000×4500 pixel photo is 10×15 inches at 300 DPI and 20×30 inches at 150 DPI. Nothing about the pixels changed — only the question being asked did.
pixelsInchesTool.printNote: The commercial standard for photos and documents viewed up close.
pixelsInchesTool.largeFormatNote: The largest size still considered sharp for a poster or banner, because it's viewed from further away.
pixelsInchesTool.screenNote: Not a property of any real screen — kept here only because the number is still widely quoted.
pixelsInchesTool.noDpiHeading: Why a screen doesn't have a DPI
pixelsInchesTool.noDpiBody: DPI measures dots printed per inch of paper — it only exists once ink meets a fixed physical size. A screen has no fixed dot pitch in that sense: the same 1920×1080 image looks denser on a small phone panel than on a large monitor, and neither number is stored anywhere in the file. The '72 DPI' people quote for screens is not a measurement of any display; it's a print-era convention that outlived the product it described.

pixelsInchesTool.tagline: Pixel size to physical size, and the largest honest print.

printCropTool.title: Photo Print Sizes Crop Calculator — Free
printCropTool.description: See exactly how much of a photo gets cropped printing 6x4, 5x7, 8x10, A4 and more — by size, in inches or centimetres, with the cut shown on the frame.
printCropTool.h1: How much your photo loses at each print size
printCropTool.answer: A 3:2 photo — the shape from almost every dedicated camera — prints whole on a 6x4 (or its metric twin, 10x15cm): both are the same 3:2 shape, so 0% is cropped. Move that photo to a 5x7 and it loses 6.7% off one pair of edges; to an 8x10, 16.7%. A 4:3 phone photo runs the other way, losing 11.1% on a 6x4 but only 6.3% on an 8x10, because 8x10 (1.25:1) sits closer to 4:3 (1.33:1) than 6x4 (1.5:1) does.
printCropTool.fact1: 6x4 and its metric twin, 10x15cm, are the same 3:2 shape — the metric print is sold under that name because 15:10 reduces to the same ratio as 6:4, not because the centimetres match the inches.
printCropTool.fact2: One shape crops from opposite edges on different prints: a 4:3 photo loses height on a 6x4 and width on an 8x10, because 6x4 is wider than 4:3 and 8x10 is narrower than it.
printCropTool.fact3: A4's shape (1:1.414, fixed by the ISO 216 paper standard) sits almost exactly at the geometric mean of 4:3 and 3:2, so a 4:3 phone photo and a 3:2 camera photo both lose about the same 5.7% printing to A4 — just off different edges.
printCropTool.fact4: 8x10 and 10x8 are the same sheet of paper sold under both digit orders, so any photo loses an identical amount on either — the test suite for this tool asserts that the two never disagree.
printCropTool.noCrop: 0% — this shape already matches the print, nothing is cut
printCropTool.frameAlt: A {source} photo cropped to fill a {print} print
printCropTool.tagline: What a 3:2 or 4:3 photo loses on 6x4, 5x7, 8x10 and A4.

screenSizeTool.title: Screen size calculator: width and height by diagonal
screenSizeTool.description: Enter a diagonal and aspect ratio to get exact width, height and area in inches or centimetres — and see what a wider ratio quietly gives up.
screenSizeTool.answer: A screen's diagonal alone does not tell you its width or height — you also need the aspect ratio. A 34-inch 16:9 screen is about 29.6 by 16.7 inches. The same 34-inch diagonal at a nominal 21:9 is about 31.3 inches wide and only 13.4 inches tall, 19.7% less height from a spec that looks identical; on a real 3440 x 1440 ultrawide it is 21.2% less. Width = diagonal x ratio / sqrt(ratio squared + 1); height = diagonal / sqrt(ratio squared + 1).
screenSizeTool.fact1: At a 5-unit diagonal, a 4:3 screen is exactly 4 by 3 — the check comes out exact rather than rounded because 3-4-5 is a Pythagorean triple.
screenSizeTool.fact2: The formula needs only the diagonal and the ratio r = width ÷ height: height = diagonal ÷ √(r² + 1), width = height × r. No trigonometry and no per-ratio lookup table.
screenSizeTool.fact3: Two screens with the same diagonal are not the same size: at 34 inches, 16:9 holds about 494 square inches, 21:9 about 419, and 32:9 about 301 — the wider the ratio, the more area a fixed diagonal gives up.
screenSizeTool.invalidDiagonal: Enter a diagonal greater than zero.
screenSizeTool.compareHeading: The same {d} {unit} diagonal, five different rectangles
screenSizeTool.surprise: At a {d} {unit} diagonal, 16:9 gives you {h169} {unit} of height and {a169} {unit}² of area. 21:9 at the exact same diagonal gives only {h219} {unit} of height and {a219} {unit}² of area — {pctHeight} less height and {pctArea} less area, from a diagonal spec that reads as identical.

sensorCropTool.title: Sensor Size Comparison & Crop Factor Calculator
sensorCropTool.description: See the exact crop factor between full frame, APS-C, Micro Four Thirds and more — plus the 35mm-equivalent focal length and aperture.
sensorCropTool.answer: Crop factor is a full-frame sensor's 43.27 mm diagonal divided by a smaller sensor's own diagonal: an APS-C Canon sensor's 26.82 mm diagonal gives a crop factor of 1.613×. That factor scales both numbers a lens produces — a 50 mm lens frames like an 80.7 mm lens would on full frame, and f/2.8 behaves like f/4.52 for how much of the scene stays in focus. Only the framing and the depth of field change; exposure does not, because it is set by the lens's actual f-number on any sensor size.
sensorCropTool.fact1: Crop factor is computed by Pythagoras from each sensor's published width and height, then dividing the full-frame diagonal (43.27 mm) by the sensor's own — nothing here is a memorised lookup table.
sensorCropTool.fact2: Full frame's own diagonal divided by itself has to equal exactly 1.000×; that identity is the check that the formula is doing the work, not a table of copied numbers.
sensorCropTool.fact3: Equivalent aperture (crop factor × f-number) changes depth of field, never exposure — a lens's actual f-number still sets how much light reaches any sensor, regardless of its size.
sensorCropTool.fact4: Micro Four Thirds computes to a 1.999× crop factor and the 1-inch sensor to 2.727×, both matching the figures those formats are already known by — independent confirmation the arithmetic tracks the real world.
sensorCropTool.diagramAlt: Full frame, APS-C, Micro Four Thirds, 1-inch and medium format sensors drawn to scale and centred on one another
sensorCropTool.exposureNote: This changes depth of field, not exposure: the lens is still f/{aperture} for how much light reaches the sensor, on any format. A larger sensor does gather more total light at that same f-number — that is a separate story about noise, not exposure.
sensorCropTool.fullFrameNote: Full frame is the reference sensor: its own diagonal divided by itself has to come out to exactly 1.000× — the check that this is arithmetic, not a lookup table.
